topics.name: Intro & price mechanism
topics.notes:
Scarcity is the central economic problem: limited factors of production (labour, land and raw materials, capital) against unlimited wants.

Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone. At the margin means comparing the extra benefit with the extra cost of one more unit.

Price mechanism:

  • Shortage (QD > QS) → price rises until QD = QS
  • Surplus (QD < QS) → price falls until QD = QS
topics.why: Short and conceptual. Read the notes once, then drill.

topics.name: Demand & supply
topics.notes:
Law of demand: P↑ → Qd↓. It works through the substitution effect (buy less of the now-dearer good and more of others) and the income effect (real income falls, so buy less).

Trap: own price change = movement along the curve. Anything else = shift.

Demand shifts RIGHT when: substitute price↑, complement price↓, income↑ (normal good), favourable tastes, expected future price↑, population↑. The reverse shifts it left.

Supply shifts RIGHT when: costs↓, alternative products less profitable, joint-supply good more profitable, favourable events (weather), expected future price ↓. The reverse shifts it left.

Trap: an expected future price rise shifts demand right but supply left. Firms hold back stock to sell later.

VAT or tax on a good → supply left. Subsidy → supply right.
topics.why: It's all about which way curves shift. Flashcards until the shift rules are automatic.

Price ceiling = legal maximum, effective only below equilibrium. It causes a shortage, so goods are allocated by queuing or rationing, which leads to black markets. It also costs money to administer and enforce. Justified to keep prices low in war, famine or for social reasons. Hurts suppliers.

Price floor = legal minimum, effective only above equilibrium. It causes a surplus, which the government often has to buy and then dispose of. Costs money to administer. Justified to protect supplier incomes, build stocks for future shortages, or support industries.
topics.why: Questions give you a schedule and ask for equilibrium, shortage or surplus. Practise the numbers.

topics.name: Elasticity
topics.notes:
PED = ΔQ/ΔP × (P1+P2)/(Q1+Q2) (arc / midpoint method)

The sign shows direction: negative means the good follows the law of demand. The size shows responsiveness: |PED| > 1 is elastic, < 1 is inelastic, = 1 is unit elastic.

Worked example (2024/25 paper): €150 → 60 clients, €200 → 50 clients. −10/50 × 350/110 = −0.2 × 3.18 = −0.64, so inelastic.

Determinants of PED: number and closeness of substitutes, share of income spent, time period, habits and brand loyalty.

PES determinants: how fast MC rises, time period, spare capacity and stocks, resource mobility.
topics.why: Arc PED comes up on every past paper. Do calculations until you don't need to think about the formula.

topics.name: Production & costs
topics.notes:
Short run: at least one factor is fixed. Long run: all factors are variable.

Diminishing marginal returns (short run): adding a variable factor to a fixed one eventually makes marginal output fall. This makes MC rise. Before that, increasing returns make MC fall, so MC is U-shaped.

TC = TFC + TVC AC = TC/Q AFC = TFC/Q MC = ΔTC

MC cuts AC at AC's minimum. AFC falls continuously.

Returns to scale (long run): double the inputs and output more than doubles (increasing), exactly doubles (constant), or less than doubles (decreasing).

Internal economies: specialisation of labour, indivisibilities and the container principle, bigger machines, by-products, organisational economies, spreading overheads and R&D, financial economies (cheaper borrowing, bulk buying).

External economies (benefit the whole industry): marketing agencies, trade fairs, shared R&D, infrastructure.

Internal diseconomies: harder to coordinate, alienated workers, industrial relations problems. External: pressure on infrastructure, labour or raw material shortages.
topics.why: Cost tables (TC, MC, AC) are guaranteed marks. Drill them, then flashcard the economies of scale.

topics.name: Revenue & profit
topics.notes:
Price taker (horizontal demand): P = AR = MR.

With a downward-sloping demand curve, MR lies below AR. TR is at its maximum where MR = 0.

Profit maximisation: MR = MC, or equivalently where the vertical gap between TR and TC is greatest.

Normal profit is the minimum needed to keep the entrepreneur in the industry (AR = AC). Supernormal profit is anything above that (AR > AC).
topics.why: TR and MR tables plus the MR = MC rule. Short topic, mostly numbers.

Perfect competition: short run P = MC, with supernormal profit or loss possible. In the long run entry competes profit away, giving P = MC = min AC. Advantages: normal profit only, low prices, consumer sovereignty, efficiency, no advertising. Disadvantages: too little profit for investment, no variety, no competition over design.

Monopoly: one firm, no close substitutes, barriers to entry, controls price or quantity but not both. Barriers include economies of scale, brand loyalty, control of factors or outlets, legal restrictions, mergers, aggressive tactics, and natural monopoly. Against: P > MC, higher price, lower output, inefficient, weak incentive to innovate, less choice. For: economies of scale, no wasteful duplication, survives recessions, no need to advertise, R&D funding.

Monopolistic competition: short run MR = MC. Long run MR = MC and AR = AC (normal profit, tangency). Advantages: variety, innovation, competition. Disadvantages: inefficient resource use, competitive advertising.

Oligopoly: interdependence and barriers to entry. Collusion is favoured by few firms, similar products and methods, entry barriers, a stable market, and legality. A cartel restricts output to where industry MR = MC. In the kinked demand model, rivals match price cuts but not rises, so there's a gap in MR and prices stay stable even when MC changes.

Game theory: in the prisoner's dilemma, each player's dominant strategy (confess, or cut price) leaves both worse off than cooperating.
topics.why: Lots of assumptions and pros and cons to memorise. Flashcards first.

topics.name: Consumer behaviour
topics.notes:
Utility: total, average, and marginal (extra satisfaction from one more unit). The rational choice model says people pick a most-preferred option from those available.

  • Framing: presentation changes the choice (shampoo, 200 saved vs 400 die). Menu or decoy effects (Economist print-only option, TV display).
  • Anchoring and defaults: irrelevant reference points (UN wheel), default options.
  • Herding: bandwagon effects in stocks, restaurants, music, ratings.
  • Uncertainty: overweighting small samples, apophenia, overweighting low-probability events (Lotto, fear of flying). Linda problem: the conjunction can't be more likely than its part.
  • Loss aversion: losses hurt more than equal gains please (free trials). Sunk cost fallacy (Arkes & Blumer).
  • Confidence and social norms: dictator game vs ultimatum game, where the responder can reject.
  • Time: present bias, remedied by precommitment (Ulysses, Clocky). Projection bias means judging the future by current tastes.
topics.why: Each bias has a name and a classic example. Match them with flashcards.

questions.q: What do economists call the central economic problem?
questions.e: Resources (labour, land and raw materials, capital) are limited relative to wants. That's scarcity.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
o: The money price paid for a good
The total cost of all alternatives
The value of the next best alternative forgone
The cost of producing one extra unit
questions.e: Opportunity cost is the best alternative you give up when you make a choice.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a factor of production?
questions.e: Money is a medium of exchange, not a productive resource. Capital means machines, buildings and tools.

questions.q: "Decisions are made at the margin" means people:
o: Weigh the extra benefit against the extra cost of one more unit
Make decisions based on total utility
questions.e: Marginal thinking compares the additional benefit and additional cost of a small change.

questions.q: If the market price is below equilibrium, there will be:
o: A surplus and price will fall
A shortage and price will rise
A surplus and price will rise
A shortage and price will fall
questions.e: Below equilibrium, QD > QS, so there's a shortage. Competition among buyers pushes price up until QD = QS.

questions.q: If QD < QS at the current price, the price mechanism will:
questions.e: QD < QS is a surplus. Sellers cut prices to clear stock, which eliminates the surplus.

questions.q: The law of demand states that, other things being equal:
o: As price rises, quantity demanded rises
As price rises, quantity demanded falls
questions.e: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related, so the demand curve slopes downward.

questions.q: The law of supply states that, other things being equal:
o: As price rises, quantity supplied falls
As price rises, quantity supplied rises
questions.e: Higher prices make it worth incurring extra unit costs and switching resources from less profitable goods.

questions.q: The substitution effect says that when the price of a good rises, consumers will buy:
o: More of the good because real income has fallen
More of the dearer good and less of others
Less of the dearer good and more of some other good
Less of the good because real income has fallen
questions.e: The good is now relatively more expensive, so people switch to alternatives. Option D describes the income effect.

questions.q: The income effect says that when the price of a good rises, consumers will buy:
o: Less of the good because their real income is lower
More of the good because their real income is lower
Less of the dearer good and more of another good
The same amount because income is unchanged
questions.e: A price rise reduces purchasing power (real income), so people buy less.

questions.q: A change in the price of the good itself causes:
o: A movement along the demand curve
A shift of both demand and supply
questions.e: Own price → movement along the curve. Any other determinant changing → shift of the curve.

questions.q: Which would shift the demand curve for a good to the RIGHT?
o: A rise in the price of a complement
A rise in the price of a substitute
An expectation that its price will fall
questions.e: If substitutes get dearer, people switch to this good. The other three all shift demand left.

questions.q: The price of a complementary good falls. Demand for the original good:
questions.e: Complements are used together, e.g. cheaper petrol raises demand for cars.

questions.q: Which would shift the demand curve for a normal good to the LEFT?
o: An expectation of future price increases
questions.e: Lower income → less demand for normal goods. Expected future price rises shift demand right because people buy now.

questions.q: Which would shift the supply curve to the LEFT?
o: A fall in the cost of production
A rise in the cost of production
A rise in the price of the good
questions.e: Higher costs make each unit less profitable, so less is supplied at every price. A price change is a movement along the curve, not a shift.

questions.q: Firms expect the price of their product to RISE in the future. Current supply:
questions.e: Firms hold back stock to sell later at the higher price, so supply today shifts left. Expect a future price fall and supply shifts right.

questions.q: Alternative products a firm could make become more profitable. Supply of the original good:
questions.e: Resources move to the more profitable alternative, so supply of the original good falls.

questions.q: A good in JOINT supply becomes more profitable (e.g. beef → more hides). Supply of the original good:
questions.e: Producing more of one automatically produces more of the other, so supply shifts right.

questions.q: An increase in VAT on a good will shift its:
questions.e: A tax on the good is a determinant of supply. It raises the cost to sellers, so supply shifts left.

questions.q: Which statement about the market demand curve is FALSE?
o: It may shift if the price of the product itself changes
It may shift if the number of consumers changes
It may shift if household behaviour changes
It is the sum of all individual demand curves
questions.e: A change in the product's own price is a movement along the curve, never a shift. This one is lifted from the Demand tutorial sheet.

questions.q: Sony TV demand: €200 → 8,800 units, €240 → 8,000 units (linear). What is quantity demanded at €225?
questions.e: Demand falls by 800 per €40, i.e. 20 units per €1. €25 above €200 → 8,800 − 500 = 8,300.

questions.q: Concert tickets (lecture table): at €40, QD = 500k and QS = 200k. This means:
questions.e: QD − QS = 500k − 200k = 300,000 shortage. This matches the Markets in Action slide.

questions.q: Why does the supply curve slope upward?
o: Consumers want more at higher prices
At higher prices it's worth incurring higher extra costs, and firms switch from less profitable goods
questions.e: Straight from the supply slides. Also, in the long run higher prices attract new firms.
Equilibrium is where QD = QS: both are 350,000 at €60.

questions.q: Same concert table: at €80, QD = 200k and QS = 530k. There is:
questions.e: QS − QD = 530k − 200k = 330,000 surplus. Price will fall.

questions.q: Demand increases (shifts right) while supply is unchanged. Equilibrium price and quantity:
questions.e: Movement up along the existing supply curve to a new higher P and higher Q.

questions.q: Supply increases (shifts right) while demand is unchanged. Equilibrium price and quantity:
questions.e: Movement down along the demand curve, giving a lower price and higher quantity.

questions.q: Health concerns emerge about soft drinks. In the Coca-Cola market:
o: Demand shifts left; price and quantity fall
questions.e: Tastes move away from the product, so demand falls and both P and Q fall.

questions.q: Coca-Cola finds a cheaper way of making Coke. In the Coke market:
o: Supply shifts right; price falls, quantity rises
questions.e: Lower production costs shift supply right.

questions.q: Tax services: P €30/40/50; QD 14/11/8 (000 hrs); QS 6/11/15. The equilibrium is:
questions.e: QD = QS = 11,000 hours at €40.

questions.q: Footballs: at €6, QD = 60 and QS = 20 (equilibrium €8, 40). The market has:
questions.e: QD − QS = 40 excess demand. Price is bid up toward €8.

questions.q: A price ceiling is:
o: A minimum price set by government
A maximum price set by government
questions.e: Ceiling = maximum price. Floor = minimum price.

questions.q: To have any effect, a price ceiling must be set:
questions.e: A maximum price above equilibrium doesn't bind, since the market price is already lower.

questions.q: An effective price ceiling creates:
questions.e: Below equilibrium, QD > QS, so there's a shortage that must be allocated by queuing or rationing.

questions.q: Which is a typical consequence of rationing under a price ceiling?
questions.e: From the slides: rationing creates a black market. Price controls also cost money to administer and enforce.

questions.q: An effective price floor (minimum price) leads to:
questions.e: Set above equilibrium, QS > QD, so there's a surplus. The government often has to buy it.

questions.q: A justification for a price floor given in the lectures is:
o: To keep prices low in wartime
questions.e: Floors protect producers' incomes (e.g. farmers). Ceilings are justified by keeping prices low in war or famine.

questions.q: Which is a justification for a price CEILING?
o: Keep prices low during war or famine
questions.e: The other three options are floor justifications.

questions.q: A ban on international travel during a pandemic. Market for holidays in Thailand:
o: Demand shifts left; price and quantity fall
questions.e: Tourists can't travel, so demand collapses and both P and Q fall.

questions.q: Universal Studios opens a theme park in Paris. Market for Eurodisney tickets:
o: Demand shifts left; P and Q fall
questions.e: A new close substitute pulls demand away from Eurodisney.

questions.q: The government subsidises indoor leisure centres. Market for admission:
o: Supply shifts right; price falls, quantity rises
questions.e: A subsidy lowers producers' costs, the opposite of a tax, so supply shifts right.

questions.q: Price elasticity of demand measures:
o: How much price changes when demand changes
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price
The slope of the supply curve
questions.e: PED = % change in Qd ÷ % change in P.

questions.q: The arc (midpoint) formula for PED used in lectures is:
questions.e: ΔQ/ΔP × mid-P/mid-Q, which is the same thing since the ÷2s cancel.

questions.q: Lecture example: ΔQ = 10, ΔP = −2, mid-P = 7, mid-Q = 15. PED =
You charge €150/hr with 60 clients, then €200/hr with 50 clients. Arc PED ≈
Rugby tickets: 55,000 sold at €60, 54,000 sold at €80. Arc PED ≈
World Cup tickets: 5,000 sold at €20, 4,500 sold at €30. Arc PED ≈
A negative PED tells you that the good:
questions.e: The sign shows direction: price and quantity move in opposite directions, which is the law of demand. The size (>1 or <1) tells you elastic or inelastic.

questions.q: If demand is price ELASTIC, a price increase will cause total revenue to:
questions.e: The % fall in Q outweighs the % rise in P. Elastic: P↑ TR↓, P↓ TR↑.

questions.q: If demand is price INELASTIC, a price cut will cause total revenue to:
questions.e: Q barely rises, so TR falls. Inelastic: P↑ TR↑, P↓ TR↓.

questions.q: With unit elastic demand (PED = −1), a price change leaves total revenue:
questions.e: The % changes in P and Q exactly offset.

questions.q: Which makes demand for a good MORE price elastic?
o: A small share of income spent on it
questions.e: With many substitutes, consumers switch easily when price rises.

questions.q: Demand tends to be more elastic:
o: When it's a small share of income
questions.e: Over time people find substitutes and adjust habits. Time period is one of the four determinants.

questions.q: A vertical demand curve has a PED of:
questions.e: Quantity doesn't respond at all to price. A horizontal demand curve is perfectly elastic (∞).

questions.q: A good has a NEGATIVE income elasticity of demand. It is:
questions.e: As income rises, demand falls (e.g. own-brand goods, bus travel).

questions.q: A YED greater than +1 indicates:
questions.e: Demand rises more than proportionately with income. Between 0 and 1 means a normal necessity.

questions.q: The cross-price elasticity between two goods is NEGATIVE. They are:
questions.e: B's price rises and demand for A falls, so they're used together. Positive XED means substitutes.

questions.q: Supply is likely to be MORE price elastic when:
o: There are spare capacity and stocks
The time period is very short
questions.e: Determinants of PES: how fast MC rises, time period, spare capacity and stocks, and factor mobility.

questions.q: Consumers' total expenditure on a good is equal to:
questions.e: TR = P × Q. Lecture example: €2 × 3m = €6m.

questions.q: The short run is a period in which:
o: At least one factor of production is fixed
Firms can enter and exit freely
questions.e: In the long run every factor can be varied.

questions.q: A fixed factor is:
o: An input that can't be increased in the short run
An input whose price never changes
An input used in fixed proportions
questions.e: For example a factory or machines. A variable factor (e.g. labour) can be increased in the short run.

questions.q: The law of diminishing marginal returns states that adding more of a variable factor to a fixed factor will eventually cause:
questions.e: Each extra worker eventually adds less than the previous one. This is a short-run concept only.

questions.q: Workers 0/1/2/3 produce total output 0/3/10/24. The marginal output of the 3rd worker is:
questions.e: 24 − 10 = 14. MO rises 3 → 7 → 14, which is increasing marginal returns.

questions.q: Firm X: TFC = €12; TVC at Q=4 is €28. Total cost at Q=4 is:
questions.e: TC = TFC + TVC = 12 + 28 = 40.

questions.q: Firm X: TC at Q=4 is €40 and at Q=5 is €52. The marginal cost of the 5th unit is:
Firm X: TC at Q=5 is €52. Average (total) cost at Q=5 is:
Firm X's MC per unit runs 10, 6, 5, 7, 12, 20, 31. Diminishing marginal returns set in after the:
questions.e: MC is lowest at the 3rd unit (€5) and rises from the 4th. Rising MC reflects diminishing returns.

questions.q: Fixed cost = €15. Total output 0/1/2 has VC €0/€25/€45. Average cost at 2 units is:
Fixed cost = €15. VC at 3 units is €105, at 4 units €225. MC of the 4th unit is:
questions.e: TC rises from 120 to 240, so MC = 120. FC doesn't affect MC.

questions.q: LR total cost: 0/50/90/120/160/210 for 0–5 units. The MC of the 3rd unit is:
LR total cost: 0/50/90/120/160/210 for 0–5 units. AC at 5 units is:
questions.e: 210/5 = 42. AC runs 50, 45, 40, 40, 42, so the lowest is at 3–4 units.

questions.q: The MC curve cuts the AC curve:
questions.e: When MC < AC, AC falls. When MC > AC, AC rises. So they cross at AC's lowest point.

questions.q: As output rises, average fixed cost (AFC):
questions.e: The same fixed cost is spread over more units (TFC/Q).

questions.q: The short-run MC curve first falls then rises because of:
questions.e: Short run means marginal returns. Scale economies are long run. (2022 exam Q3c)

questions.q: Doubling all inputs leads to output more than doubling. This is:
questions.e: Returns to scale apply only in the long run, when all inputs vary.

questions.q: Economies of scale exist when:
o: Total cost falls as output rises
Long-run average cost falls as output rises
questions.e: Lower cost per unit as the firm grows.

questions.q: Which is an EXTERNAL economy of scale?
o: Cheaper borrowing for a large firm
Shared infrastructure and trade fairs as the industry grows
Specialisation of labour within the firm
questions.e: External economies benefit all firms in an industry as the industry grows. The other options are internal.

questions.q: Large firms can borrow at lower interest rates. This is a:
questions.e: Financial economies are internal: cheaper borrowing and bulk discounts.

questions.q: Which is an INTERNAL DISECONOMY of scale?
o: Coordination and communication problems in a large firm
questions.e: Also alienated workers and industrial relations problems. The other three options are external diseconomies.

questions.q: The "container principle" is an example of:
o: An economy of scale from large or indivisible inputs
questions.e: Doubling a container's dimensions more than doubles its volume. Bigger machines are proportionally cheaper to run.

questions.q: For a price-taking firm (horizontal demand curve):
questions.e: Each extra unit sells at the same market price, so D = AR = MR.

questions.q: P (AR) falls 8, 7, 6, 5, 4 for units 1–5. TR = 8, 14, 18, 20, 20. MR of the 3rd unit is:
Same table (TR 8, 14, 18, 20, 20, 18, 14). Total revenue is maximised where:
questions.e: MR is 0 for the 5th unit: TR peaks at €20 when MR = 0, which is where demand is unit elastic.

questions.q: For a firm facing a downward-sloping demand curve, the MR curve:
questions.e: To sell an extra unit the firm cuts price on all units, so MR < P.

questions.q: A firm maximises profit where:
questions.e: Using total curves, this is where the vertical gap between TR and TC is greatest.

questions.q: Using total curves, profit is maximised where:
o: The vertical distance TR − TC is greatest
questions.e: Where TR and TC cross, profit is zero (break-even).

questions.q: Supernormal profit is earned when:
questions.e: Price above average cost means profit above the normal level.

questions.q: Normal profit is:
o: The minimum profit an entrepreneur will accept to stay in the industry
questions.e: Normal profit is counted as part of costs, so AR = AC means normal profit.

questions.q: Which is NOT an assumption of perfect competition?
o: No barriers to entry or exit
questions.e: Products in perfect competition are identical. Differentiation belongs to monopolistic competition.

questions.q: A perfectly competitive firm's demand curve is:
questions.e: It's a price taker: D = AR = MR at Pe.

questions.q: Why can firms in perfect competition earn only normal profit in the long run?
o: New firms enter, supply rises and price falls
questions.e: With no barriers to entry, supernormal profits attract entrants until P = minimum LRAC.

questions.q: Long-run equilibrium in perfect competition occurs where:
questions.e: LRAC = SRAC = MC = MR = AR. Firms produce at minimum AC.

questions.q: In the SHORT run, a perfectly competitive firm can:
o: Earn supernormal profit or make a loss
questions.e: Supernormal profits are competed away only in the long run.

questions.q: A disadvantage of perfect competition is:
o: Lack of product variety and insufficient profit for investment
questions.e: From the slides: insufficient profits for investment, no variety, no competition over design.

questions.q: A monopolist can control:
o: Either price or quantity, but not both
questions.e: It faces the market demand curve, so choosing P fixes Q, or vice versa.

questions.q: Which is NOT a barrier to entry?
questions.e: Perfect knowledge is a perfect-competition assumption. Other barriers include control of key factors or outlets and aggressive tactics.

questions.q: Compared with competition, a monopoly typically results in:
questions.e: The monopolist sets MR = MC where P > MC.

questions.q: A monopolist can earn supernormal profit in the LONG run because:
o: Barriers to entry keep competitors out
questions.e: Without entry, profits aren't competed away.

questions.q: Which is an argument IN FAVOUR of monopoly?
o: Economies of scale and funds for R&D
questions.e: Other arguments: it avoids wasteful duplication, survives recessions, and needs no competitive advertising. Pharma is the classic R&D example.

questions.q: Which is an assumption of monopolistic competition?
o: Product differentiation with no barriers to entry
questions.e: Many sellers, close but differentiated substitutes, independent firms, free entry, and non-price competition.

questions.q: Long-run equilibrium in monopolistic competition:
o: MR = MC and AR = AC (normal profit)
questions.e: Free entry removes supernormal profit, so AR is tangent to AC. But this isn't at minimum AC (excess capacity).

questions.q: A DISADVANTAGE of monopolistic competition is:
o: Inefficient use of resources and competitive advertising
Supernormal profit in the long run
questions.e: Advantages: variety, innovation, and competition lowering prices.

questions.q: A key feature of oligopoly is:
questions.e: Each firm must consider rivals' reactions. Barriers to entry exist.

questions.q: Kinked demand curve: if an oligopolist cuts its price, rivals ___; if it raises its price, rivals ___.
questions.e: So demand is elastic above the kink and inelastic below it, which keeps prices stable.

questions.q: In the kinked demand model, a change in MC between MC1 and MC2:
questions.e: There's a vertical gap in MR at the kink. Any MC passing through that gap gives the same P1 and Q1.

questions.q: Which factor makes collusion MORE likely?
o: Few firms with similar products and high entry barriers
questions.e: It also helps if firms are open with each other, have similar production methods, and collusion is legal.

questions.q: A profit-maximising cartel requires members to:
o: Restrict total output to where industry MR = MC
questions.e: The cartel behaves like a monopoly, splitting output Q1 between members.

questions.q: Firms X and Y: both £2 → £10m each; both £1.80 → £8m each; one cuts to £1.80 → cutter £12m, other £5m. The likely outcome is:
questions.e: Cutting is each firm's dominant strategy, so both end up worse off than if they'd colluded at £2.

questions.q: Prisoner's dilemma (Amanda & Nigel): neither confesses → 1 year each; both confess → 3 years each; only one confesses → 3 months for them, 10 years for the other. The likely result:
questions.e: Confessing is dominant for each player whatever the other does, so they land at 3 years each, worse than 1 year each.

questions.q: Marginal utility is:
o: The extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit
The price of the last unit
questions.e: TU = total, AU = TU/Q, MU = change in TU from one more unit.

questions.q: A choice is "rational" in the rational choice model if it is:
o: A most-preferred choice from those available
questions.e: The model works well without uncertainty, but is only an approximation.

questions.q: People pay €10 for shampoo in a salon but not in a discount supermarket. This illustrates:
questions.e: How a choice is presented (context, packaging) changes the decision.

questions.q: "Save 200 of 600 lives" vs "400 will die" produce different choices. This is:
questions.e: The outcomes are identical; only the wording (gain vs loss) differs.

questions.q: A random wheel spin influenced estimates of African countries in the UN. This shows:
questions.e: Anchoring: an irrelevant reference point affects judgement (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Default options work similarly.

questions.q: Choosing the busy restaurant over the empty one next door is an example of:
questions.e: Herding also explains stock market bubbles and online ratings effects.

questions.q: Loss aversion means people:
o: Enjoy gains more than they dislike losses
Dislike losses more than they enjoy equal gains
questions.e: Marketers use free trials so that giving the product up feels like a loss.

questions.q: Continuing a project only because of the money already spent on it is:
questions.e: Sunk costs can't be recovered, so they shouldn't affect forward-looking decisions (Arkes & Blumer, 1985).

questions.q: Present bias is the tendency to:
o: Overweight payoffs closer to the present
Rely on the first number seen
questions.e: It leads to lapses of self-control, e.g. procrastination.

questions.q: Precommitment (e.g. Ulysses tied to the mast) works by:
questions.e: It's a remedy for present bias when you don't trust your future self.

questions.q: In the ULTIMATUM game (unlike the dictator game):
o: The responder can reject, and then both get nothing
questions.e: People reject "unfair" offers even at a cost to themselves. Social norms matter.

questions.q: Projection bias is:
o: Evaluating future consequences using current tastes and needs
questions.e: E.g. shopping hungry and buying too much food.

questions.q: Overweighting a small sample ("my dad smoked and he's fine") is:
questions.e: With a large enough sample, the average resembles the population.

questions.q: Apophenia is the tendency to:
o: Perceive meaningful connections between unrelated things
questions.e: Linked in lectures to conspiracy theories under uncertainty.

questions.q: Linda example: which is more probable?
o: Linda is a bank teller AND active in the feminist movement
questions.e: A conjunction can never be more likely than one of its parts. The vivid description misleads people (availability / salience).

questions.q: The Economist offered web €59, print €125, print + web €125. The print-only option works as:
o: A decoy that makes print + web look like a bargain
questions.e: This is the menu effect: nobody picks print-only, but it shifts choices toward the bundle.

questions.q: People overweight low-probability events. This helps explain:
questions.e: It also explains fear of flying.

cards.b: Limited resources relative to unlimited wants. The central economic problem.
The value of the next best alternative forgone.
Labour, land and raw materials, capital.
QD > QS. Price rises until QD = QS.
QD < QS. Price falls until QD = QS.
As price rises, quantity demanded falls (other things equal).
As price rises, quantity supplied rises (other things equal).
Price rises, so the good is relatively dearer. Buy less of it and more of alternatives.
Price rises, so real income falls. Buy less.
Movement ALONG the curve. Never a shift.

cards.f: Six things that shift demand RIGHT
cards.b: Substitute price ↑, complement price ↓, income ↑, favourable tastes, expected future price ↑, population ↑.
Costs ↓, alternatives less profitable, joint-supply good more profitable, favourable events, expected future price ↓, subsidy.

cards.f: Expected future price rise: demand vs supply
cards.b: Demand shifts RIGHT (buy now). Supply shifts LEFT (hold stock to sell later).

cards.f: Tax or VAT on a good
cards.b: Supply shifts left.
Producing one good automatically produces another (beef and hides). One more profitable → supply of the other shifts right.
Legal MAXIMUM price. Binding only below equilibrium. Causes a shortage, then queues, rationing, black markets.
Legal MINIMUM price. Binding only above equilibrium. Causes a surplus, which the government often buys.
Keep prices low in war, famine, or for social reasons.

Responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price. %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP.
Number and closeness of substitutes, share of income spent, time period, habits and brand loyalty.
TR falls. (P↓ → TR rises)
TR rises. (P↓ → TR falls)
0 = vertical demand (perfectly inelastic). ∞ = horizontal (perfectly elastic).
Inferior / normal necessity / luxury.
Substitutes / complements.
How fast MC rises, time period, spare capacity and stocks, resource mobility.

Adding more of a variable factor to a fixed factor eventually makes marginal output fall.
Increasing marginal returns first (MC falls), then diminishing returns (MC rises).
MC cuts AC at AC's minimum.

Harder to coordinate, alienated workers, industrial relations problems.
Pressure on infrastructure, labour shortages, raw material shortages.

P = AR = MR (horizontal demand).
MR lies below AR. TR is at its maximum where MR = 0.
MR = MC (or where the vertical gap TR − TC is largest).
Normal: AR = AC, the minimum needed to stay in the industry. Supernormal: AR > AC.
Very many buyers and sellers, perfect knowledge, identical products, firms act independently, no barriers to entry or exit, profit maximisation.
P = MC = min AC, normal profit only (entry competes supernormal profit away).

written.q: Explain how price is determined in a free market.
points: Define equilibrium: the price where QD = QS
Below equilibrium: QD > QS, a shortage, so buyers bid the price up and quantity supplied rises
Above equilibrium: QS > QD, a surplus, so sellers cut prices
Price keeps adjusting until the market clears. Draw the D and S diagram with Pe and Qe labelled
Shifts in D or S create a new equilibrium (give an example)

written.q: Outline the arguments against imposing price ceilings.
points: Creates a shortage (QD > QS at the maximum price). Draw the diagram
Goods have to be allocated by queuing (wastes time) or rationing
Rationing leads to black markets
Hurts suppliers' incomes, so supply may fall further over time
Costs money to administer, organise rationing, and enforce

written.q: Outline the arguments for and against price controls.
points: For ceilings: keep essentials affordable in war, famine or crisis
For floors: protect supplier incomes, build stocks for future shortages, support industries
Against ceilings: shortages, queues, rationing, black markets, hurts suppliers
Against floors: higher consumer prices, surpluses the government must buy and dispose of
Both cost money to administer and enforce

written.q: Choose three factors which determine the price elasticity of demand for a good. Explain how each factor can determine a good's price elasticity.
points: Substitutes: more and closer substitutes make demand more elastic (example)
Share of income: a bigger share of the budget makes demand more elastic (car vs salt)
Time period: more elastic in the long run as people find alternatives
Habits and brand loyalty make demand inelastic (cigarettes, coffee)
For each: name it, explain the mechanism, give an example

written.q: €150/hr → 60 clients; €200/hr → 50 clients. Calculate PED using the midpoint method, and explain what it shows about the law of demand and relative elasticity.
points: Negative sign: P and Q move in opposite directions, so the services follow the law of demand
|PED| < 1, so demand is price inelastic: raising the price increases TR
Define: LRAC falls as output rises
Specialisation of labour: less training needed, skilled workers, no time lost switching tasks
Indivisibilities and the container principle: big machines are proportionally cheaper
Financial: cheaper borrowing, bulk-buy discounts
Organisational or overheads: R&D and admin costs spread over more units

written.q: Explain what is meant by the law of diminishing marginal returns.
points: Short run only: at least one factor is fixed
Adding more units of a variable factor (labour) to a fixed factor (machines)
Eventually marginal output, the extra output from one more unit, declines
Use the lecture table: MO 3, 7, 14, then falling
Consequence: MC starts to rise

written.q: Explain why the short-run marginal cost curve slopes downwards initially but eventually slopes upwards.
points: MC = change in TC from one more unit
At first, increasing marginal returns: each worker adds more output, so cost per extra unit falls
Then diminishing marginal returns set in, each worker adds less, so MC rises
Draw the U-shaped MC curve cutting AC at its minimum

written.q: Outline the advantages and disadvantages (from society's perspective) of competitive markets.
points: Advantages: only normal profit in the long run, P = MC and production at min AC (efficient)
Low prices, consumer sovereignty, responsive to consumer wishes, no wasteful advertising
Disadvantages: too little profit for investment or R&D
Lack of product variety (identical products)
No competition over product design and specification

written.q: Outline the ways in which monopolistic competition may be more beneficial to society than monopoly.
points: No supernormal profit in the long run (free entry)
Lower prices and higher output than a monopoly
More consumer choice through product differentiation
Competition drives efficiency and innovation
Monopolies can stay inefficient and still survive behind barriers

written.q: Outline the advantages that monopolies can sometimes have for societies.
points: Economies of scale can mean lower costs or prices
Avoid wasteful duplication (natural monopoly)
Survive recessions, which protects jobs
No need for competitive advertising
Supernormal profits fund R&D (pharmaceuticals)
